text: Tachycardia ● Heart is beating too fast ● If too fast, poor perfusion to cardiac myocytes (via coronary arteries), brain, other vital organs ● Causes include: ○ Physiologic/abnormal automaticity ○ Re-entry (e.g. atrial flutter) ○ Triggered activity (e.g. atrial fibrillation) ○ Structural remodeling (e.g. scar-mediated ventricular tachycardia’s) ○ Genetic (e.g. ARVC – arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy)

text: Atrial Flutter • Regular supraventricular rhythm characterized by flutter “F” waves (sawtooth pattern) reflecting more organized atrial activity than AF​ – Rapid atrial rate of 270 to 330 bpm​ – Slower, regular electrical activity results in regular ventricular response inapproximate factors of 300 bpm​ • 2:1 conduction = ventricular rate 150 bpm (most common)​ • 3:1 conduction = ventricular rate 100 bpm​ • 4:1 conduction = ventricular rate 75 bpm

text: Arrhythmia Management • Rate Control – Class II: Beta-Blockers – Class IV: Calcium Channel Blockers (non- dihydropyridine ) • Rhythm Control – Anti-Arrhythmic Drugs (next slide) – Synchronized Cardioversion (chemical or electrical) – Defibrillation (ventricular arrhythmia) – Ablation – heat/cold • Underlying Cause/Risk Factor Reduction/Preventing Complications – Electrolyte disturbance – Hyperthyroid, sepsis, etc – Address stroke risk from atrial fibrillation & flutter (e.g. DOACs, warfarin) – Optimal therapy for comorbidities (e.g. HTN, OSA, DM) – Diet, exercise, smoking cessation, alcohol cessation/moderation

title: What is Heart Failure (HF)
text: What is Heart Failure (HF)? • It is a complex clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection of blood • Insufficient cardiac output to meet needs • NOT synonymous with cardiomyopathy • BUT, ischemic cardiomyopathy is most common cause of heart failure

title: Contraindications/Cautions: mannitol Condition Why Mannitol is Dangerous Severe renal disease / anuria (no uri
text: Contraindications/Cautions: mannitol Condition Why Mannitol is Dangerous Severe renal disease / anuria (no urine output) If the kidneys can’t make urine, mannitol can’t be excreted . It just stays in the bloodstream, pulling in more water into blood vessels — leading to fluid overload and worsening kidney damage . Pulmonary congestion or edema Mannitol pulls fluid from tissues into the bloodstream. If the heart or lungs are already overloaded, this extra volume can worsen pulmonary edema (fluid in the lungs) and cause shortness of breath or hypoxia . Dehydration Mannitol causes further water loss through diuresis, which can make dehydration much worse and cause electrolyte imbalances or hypotension. Heart failure (HF) In HF, the heart can’t pump effectively. Mannitol increases blood volume (as it pulls water from tissues), which can overwhelm the heart , leading to fluid buildup in the lungs and worsening heart failure.
